segments.say: A Moroccan sultan's Qur'an, in his own hand, at the al-Aqsa Mosque.
Another, from the royal library of al-Mansur, in Spain.
Morocco's Qur'an manuscripts are scattered across the world. Now, one guide brings them together: Masaahif al-Maghrib.
segments.show: Morocco's Qur'an manuscripts are scattered across the world. Now, one guide brings them together: Masahif al-Maghrib.

segments.say: Twelve centuries, seven dynasties, and more than sixty Qur'ans: those that survive, and those that were lost.
Some were copied by a caliph or a sultan in his own hand; others written in gold on lapis blue, or in silver on green paper.
Each one has a card that tells its story, with close-up samples of the script, and links to the digitized copies.

Prepared by Ibrahim Hassani Eedreesi, a calligrapher and manuscript researcher from Fez, who teaches Maghribi scripts, holds a Diploma in the Art of Calligraphy from al-Qarawiyyeen, and won the Encouragement Prize of the Mohammed the Sixth Award for Maghribi Calligraphy.
segments.show: Prepared by Ibrahim Hassani Idrissi, a calligrapher and manuscript researcher from Fez, who teaches Maghribi scripts, holds a Diploma in the Art of Calligraphy from al-Qarawiyyin, and won the Encouragement Prize of the Mohammed VI Award for Maghribi Calligraphy.

segments.say: A well-sourced guide, in Arabic and English, for every researcher, calligrapher, and lover of Morocco's heritage.
